title: Jeremiah 10:1–16
context: The LORD addresses the house of Israel (10:1–5), warning against learning the way of the nations and fearing idols made by craftsmen. A voice of praise answers in the second person, “There is no one like you, LORD” (10:6–7), and the poem alternates between mockery of idols (10:3–5, 8–9, 14–15) and praise of the living God (10:6–7, 10, 12–13, 16). Verse 10:11 is widely recognized as the only verse in Jeremiah written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew; interpreters differ on why, and the question is not settled here. Verses 10:12–16 closely parallel 51:15–19; the two are named here without harmonizing their small differences. Both traditions read the passage as a confession that the LORD alone is the Creator and King, and that idols are powerless.

verses.text: Hear the word which the LORD speaks to you, house of Israel!
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah calls the house of Israel to hear the word the LORD speaks to them. Arminian readers note that the oracle begins with an appeal to listen, assuming hearers who can heed or ignore the word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call to hear as the LORD addressing his covenant people with authority. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a sustained contrast between the living God and idols, spoken to Israel for its instruction.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD warns them not to learn the way of the nations or be dismayed at signs in the sky. Arminian readers see a call to resist cultural pressure toward fear-based religion that surrounding peoples practiced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the nations’ terror at heavenly signs reflects worship of the creation rather than the Creator. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as freeing God’s people from fear of omens and astral powers.

verses.text: For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax.
verses.arminianNotes: The customs of the peoples are vanity: a tree is cut from the forest and shaped by a workman’s ax. Arminian readers note the irony that worshipers make with their own hands the thing they then fear and serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing idolatry’s absurdity, worshiping what human skill has made. Both traditions read the satire as a reminder that the true God is not crafted, and they note similar mockery in Isaiah 44:9–20 by reference.

verses.text: They deck it with silver and with gold. They fasten it with nails and with hammers, so that it can’t move.
verses.arminianNotes: The idol is decked with silver and gold and fastened with nails so it cannot move. Arminian readers note the humor: the god must be nailed down to keep it from falling over, unable to stand on its own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the costly decoration as showing that wealth cannot give life to a lifeless object. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as satire that strips idols of the power their worshipers imagine.

verses.text: They are like a palm tree, of turned work, and don’t speak. They must be carried, because they can’t move. Don’t be afraid of them; for they can’t do evil, neither is it in them to do good.”
verses.arminianNotes: Idols are like a palm tree of turned work, unable to speak or walk, so they must be carried; they can do neither evil nor good. Arminian readers see freedom from fear: such powerless things should not control anyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast with the LORD who speaks and acts, while idols are mute and helpless. Both traditions read the command not to fear idols as pastoral, releasing God’s people from the grip of empty powers.

verses.text: There is no one like you, LORD. You are great, and your name is great in might.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice of praise says there is no one like the LORD, great in himself and in the might of his name. Arminian readers see worship rising out of the contrast, turning from mockery of idols to adoration of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an affirmation of God’s incomparability, a theme central to the prophets’ confession of the one true God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise of the LORD’s unique greatness and power.

verses.text: Who shouldn’t fear you, King of the nations? For it belongs to you. Because among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their royal estate, there is no one like you.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice asks who should not fear the King of the nations, for there is none like him among the nations’ wise or royal. Arminian readers note that God’s kingship reaches beyond Israel to all peoples, who owe him reverence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s universal reign, to which all nations are accountable. Both traditions read the verse as calling every people to fear the LORD, and they find in it a wide horizon of God’s kingship.

verses.text: But they are together brutish and foolish, instructed by idols! It is just wood.
verses.arminianNotes: The idol worshipers are called brutish and foolish, instructed by what is only wood. Arminian readers see the danger that people become like what they worship, dull and senseless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing that idolatry darkens understanding, so that instruction from idols yields only folly. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a warning that false worship corrupts the mind.

verses.text: There is silver beaten into plates, which is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the engraver and of the hands of the goldsmith. Their clothing is blue and purple. They are all the work of skillful men.
verses.arminianNotes: Silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, worked by engravers and goldsmiths, clothe the idols in blue and purple. Arminian readers note the expense and skill lavished on objects that remain mere products of human craft.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing that idols, however splendid, are only the work of skillful men. Both traditions read the list of materials as underlining the futility of idolatry; the location of Uphaz is uncertain and it is not identified here.

verses.text: But the LORD is the true God. He is the living God, and an everlasting King. At his wrath, the earth trembles. The nations aren’t able to withstand his indignation.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD is the true and living God and an everlasting King, at whose wrath the earth trembles. Arminian readers see the decisive contrast: the LORD lives and acts, while idols are lifeless works of human hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an affirmation of God’s eternal sovereignty and holy wrath before which the nations cannot stand. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a confession of the LORD’s life, truth, and kingship.

verses.text: “You shall say this to them: ‘The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth will perish from the earth, and from under the heavens.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Israel is told what to say to the nations: gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish. Arminian readers note that the verse, commonly recognized as written in Aramaic, equips God’s people to answer outsiders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as summarizing the creation-based case against idols, compare 10:12. Both traditions read the saying as a confession of the Creator over false gods; why it stands in Aramaic is debated, and the notes leave that question open.

verses.text: God has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding has he stretched out the heavens.
verses.arminianNotes: God made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens. Arminian readers see creation as the work of a wise and powerful God who stands over all he has made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verse the doctrine of creation as the foundation of God’s lordship. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grounding worship in God’s creative power; 51:15 offers a close parallel.

verses.text: When he utters his voice, the waters in the heavens roar, and he causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth. He makes lightnings for the rain, and brings the wind out of his treasuries.
verses.arminianNotes: When God speaks, the waters roar; he raises vapors, makes lightning for rain, and brings wind from his treasuries. Arminian readers see God’s active, ongoing care for the world he made, sustaining its weather and life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence governing natural forces, which do not run apart from him. Both traditions read the verse as celebrating the LORD as Lord of storm and rain, the very things idolaters credited to other gods.

verses.text: Every man has become brutish and without knowledge. Every goldsmith is disappointed by his engraved image; for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone has become brutish and without knowledge; the goldsmith is disappointed by his image, for there is no breath in it. Arminian readers note the shame of trusting what cannot answer or save.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lack of breath as the decisive mark of idols, which have no life to give. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that idols fail those who trust them; 51:17 offers a close parallel.

verses.text: They are vanity, a work of delusion. In the time of their visitation they will perish.
verses.arminianNotes: Idols are vanity and a work of delusion, and in the time of their visitation they will perish. Arminian readers see the end of idols as part of God’s judgment, exposing their emptiness before all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming that God will bring every false god to nothing. Both traditions read the line as certainty that idols have no future, and they note its near repetition in 51:18.

verses.text: The portion of Jacob is not like these; for he is the maker of all things; and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance. The LORD of Armies is his name.
verses.arminianNotes: The portion of Jacob is not like idols, for he is the maker of all things, and Israel is his inheritance. Arminian readers see covenant belonging: Israel’s portion is the living God, and they are his own people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a mutual possession, God as Israel’s portion and Israel as God’s inheritance, grounded in his choice. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a joyful confession of covenant relationship with the Creator.
